summary: Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, for adjudication of disputes between DVC and PSPCL and for directions. - _(e) pass such further order or orders as this Hon’ble Commission may deem just and proper in the circumstances of the case.”_ 8. The Petitioner has filed Written Submissions dated 12.7.2025 on the question of arbitrability of the disputes and has mainly submitted the following: l. Objections relating to lack of jurisdiction and arbitrability can be raised at any stage of the proceedings, including collateral proceedings, and are required to be examined at the threshold. 9. PSPCL, in its response dated 14.8.2025 filed to the Written Submissions filed by the Petitioner dated 12.7.2025 on the question of arbitrability of the disputes, has mainly submitted the following: a. The Petitioner had itself, during the hearings held on 21.1.2025 and 25.3.2025, requested that the present matter be taken up after the decision in batch matters concerning arbitrability of tariff and non-tariff disputes, and subsequently sought time on 13.5.2025 to file Written Submissions on arbitrability, which indicates that the issue is not settled in the manner sought to be projected by the Petitioner. b. The reliance placed by the Petitioner on the judgment of MPPMCL v. DVC and the affirmation thereof by the DVC Supreme Court Order is misplaced and requires proper appreciation in the context of the facts and issues involved in the present case. The said judgment deals with the issue of arbitrability in the context of disputes relating to termination of PPA and the applicability of Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, in proceedings under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act, and lays down the distinction between tariff and non-tariff disputes. e. The contention of the Petitioner that disputes relating to fixed charges can be treated as non-tariff disputes is erroneous, as fixed charges are inseparable from tariff and cannot be viewed in isolation as purely contractual claims. The comparison sought to be drawn by the Petitioner between the present case and the DVC APTEL case is incorrect and misleading, inasmuch as the primary issue in the DVC APTEL case pertained to the termination of the PPA, whereas the present case concerns the payment of fixed charges forming part of the tariff. 10. We have examined the rival contentions. Petitioner’s contention is that the dispute is contractual in nature and it constitutes a non-tariff dispute; on the contrary, PSPCL’s contention is that the present dispute is a tariff dispute and has to be adjudicated by the Commission. Thus, the limited issue before us at this stage is whether the dispute raised by the Petitioner in the present Petition constitutes a tariffrelated dispute or a non-tariff dispute and whether the same falls under the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act? ## 18. Clause 6 of the PPA provides for a dispute resolution mechanism, and it is as _The power conferred on the Central Commission to adjudicate disputes is confined only to those disputes involving (1) generating companies or (2) transmission licensees. As long as the dispute involves a generating company or a transmission licensee, and even if the other parties to the dispute are neither generating companies nor transmission licensees, the Central Commission would have jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes._ 30. In view of the above, since the issue raised in the present proceedings relates to fixed/ capacity charges, which constitute a component of the tariff, it falls within the regulatory domain of the tariff. We take note of the submission of the Petitioner that disputes arising out of alleged contractual breaches under the PPA, which do not impact tariff determination or regulation, fall outside the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission, while relying on the judgment of the APTEL in MPPMCL v. DVC. However, in light of the subsequent judgment in the Mundra UMPP batch, the earlier reliance placed on the judgment dated 28.8.2024 in MPPMCL v. DVC no longer advances the case of the Petitioner. The law now stands clarified that disputes relating to the regulatory functions of the Commission, or which impact tariff either directly or indirectly, are non-arbitrable, notwithstanding an arbitration agreement. It is also observed that though the Petitioner has characterised the dispute as arising from nonscheduling of power and consequent contractual breach, the nature of the relief sought is determinative. Even though non-scheduling may arise from contractual conduct, the consequence sought, namely the recovery of fixed/capacity charges, is governed by tariff principles and forms an integral part of the tariff framework regulated by the Commission. 32. In view of the foregoing analysis, the Commission holds that the present Petition raises a tariff-related dispute falling squarely within the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act. The Commission is empowered and duty-bound to adjudicate the dispute on the merits and is not required to refer it to arbitration.
title: Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, for adjudication of disputes between DVC and PSPCL and for directions. Damodar Valley Corporation
